Insurance terms · Plain English

What does ‘sum insured’ mean on your policy schedule?

The number looks simple. What it does depends on the asset, the valuation basis and the wording beside it.

Quick answer The sum insured is the amount shown for a particular section of your policy and usually acts as the maximum or reference amount for a valid claim. It is not a guaranteed payout: the insurer still applies the proven loss, valuation basis, excess, limits, exclusions, conditions and the policy wording. A current SAIA/National Financial Ombud explainer makes the same distinction for home contents.

Sum insured meaning, in one clear sentence

Your sum insured is the value recorded against a policy section, asset or financial interest, used as a cap or calculation reference when the insurer assesses a valid claim. The policy schedule is the summary; the full wording tells you how the number works. Standard Bank’s insurance-contract glossary similarly describes the schedule as the quick reference for what is covered and the sum insured as the maximum for a specific claim.

The number should normally match the policy’s stated valuation basis. That may be full reinstatement cost for a building, new-replacement cost for household contents, a defined vehicle value, the correct value of business stock or a forward-looking gross-profit amount. It is therefore possible for two sections on the same schedule to use the same label but require very different calculations.

Read three things together: the item on the schedule, its basis of settlement in the wording, and any limit or sublimit that applies. A high overall sum insured does not cancel a lower single-item limit.

The number is not your premium, excess or promised payout

Several amounts live on an insurance schedule, but they do different jobs. Confusing them can make a quote look stronger, or a claim look more certain, than it really is.

Sum insured compared with related insurance terms
TermPlain-English meaningRelationship to the sum insured
PremiumThe price you pay to keep the cover in force.A sum insured can affect the premium, but the two amounts are not interchangeable.
ExcessThe first amount or contribution you carry on an accepted claim.It may be deducted from the calculated settlement; it does not change the schedule’s sum insured.
Claim amountThe value of the loss you report and support with evidence.It is assessed against the policy rules and cap; it is not automatically paid in full.
Replacement valueWhat it costs to replace or reinstate on the policy’s stated basis at current prices.Often the target amount for buildings, contents and equipment sums insured.
Market valueA current value under a defined market-based method.It may be the settlement basis for some vehicles or assets, but not for a replacement-value building.
Agreed valueAn amount accepted in advance for an eligible item, often with a valuation.It can be the stated insured value, but eligibility, review and settlement conditions still come from the policy.
Indemnity valueA value intended to restore the insured’s financial position, sometimes after depreciation.The settlement may be lower than a new-replacement sum insured if the wording uses an indemnity basis.
Limit or sublimitA separate ceiling for a benefit, item, category, event or policy period.It can cap part of a claim below the overall sum insured.

The distinction matters most at claim stage. Sasria’s 2026 Material Damage Policy, for example, says the insured may claim only the value of the loss suffered, subject to the limit of indemnity, even where the represented sum insured is higher.

One label, different jobs across six types of cover

The correct sum insured depends on what the section protects. Use the schedule as the map, then check the wording’s valuation rules before choosing or updating the number.

How the valuation basis commonly changes by insurance class
Cover classWhat the amount commonly representsImportant check
BuildingsFull reinstatement cost of the insured structures, not the land or sale price.Include the costs the wording requires, which may extend to demolition, professional fees, municipal costs and escalation.
Household contentsThe total current cost to replace insured belongings, commonly with equivalent new items.Complete a room-by-room home inventory and inspect item or category sublimits.
MotorA policy-defined retail, market, trade or agreed value.Read the current value type and method; it may change over time and is not necessarily purchase price or finance balance.
Business assets or stockReplacement, market, cost or another stated basis for equipment, plant, stock and other property.Stock declarations, seasonal peaks, installation and transport costs may matter.
Business interruptionA financial amount such as gross profit, revenue or standing charges over the indemnity period.Forecast growth and the full indemnity period rather than copying last year’s accounting figure.
Public liabilityUsually a “limit of indemnity” per event and sometimes in aggregate for the period.Check whether defence costs sit inside or outside the limit and whether lower sublimits apply.

For buildings, the Association of South African Quantity Surveyors says the sum insured should be based on a full replacement-cost valuation rather than market or investment value, and recommends a professional quantity surveyor for a reliable assessment. Its reinstatement guidance includes demolition, professional fees, local-authority costs and escalation.

Motor values work differently. A current South African vehicle-value explainer distinguishes retail, market, trade and agreed value, and stresses that the specific coversheet and wording control. Commercial wordings can be different again: the Renasa Commercial Policy wording illustrates how stock declarations, market value and reinstatement conditions can interact.

For business interruption, the calculation is financial rather than physical. Sasria’s business-interruption overview separates gross profit, revenue, net profit, standing charges and working expenses as distinct bases of cover. This is why a schedule review should follow the asset or financial interest and the chosen wording, not one universal formula.

Why the actual payout can be lower than the sum insured

A valid claim is generally settled for the proven covered loss on the policy’s basis, up to the applicable cap. The full sum insured is therefore most relevant when the covered loss reaches that level; many ordinary claims are partial losses.

  • The loss is smaller: a R40 000 repair does not become a R500 000 payment because R500 000 appears on the schedule.
  • The basis changes the value: depreciation, market value or an indemnity basis may apply instead of new-for-old replacement.
  • An excess applies: the policyholder contributes the stated first amount, according to the wording.
  • A limit or sublimit is lower: jewellery, electronics, cash, portable items or liability benefits can have their own ceilings.
  • Underinsurance triggers average: a partial property claim may be reduced proportionally where the policy contains an average clause.
  • Terms are not met: exclusions, security requirements, maintenance provisions and other conditions can affect or defeat a claim.

SAIA’s 2026 home-contents guidance records an Ombud example in which a stolen ring’s sum insured was higher than the insurer’s supported replacement quote. The lesson was not that the schedule was ignored; it was that the sum insured was the maximum liability, while the indemnifiable replacement cost was lower. For any actual loss, use Best Care’s claims guidance and the insurer’s current process rather than relying on the number alone.

Underinsurance and the average clause, briefly

Underinsurance exists when the sum insured is below the value that should have been insured on the section’s stated basis. If the wording contains an average clause, the insurer may treat you as carrying the uninsured proportion yourself, even on a partial loss.

Illustration only: not a universal policy formula R500 000 ÷ R800 000 × R120 000 = R75 000 sum insured ÷ actual replacement value × covered loss = illustrated settlement before any applicable excess

In this example, the contents are insured for 62.5% of the R800 000 replacement value. A R120 000 covered loss is therefore reduced to R75 000 before any applicable excess. The household funds the remaining R45 000 plus the excess. The calculation mirrors the proportional approach explained by ASAQS and in Sasria’s 2026 wording, but your policy may define value at risk, tolerance, settlement and deductions differently.

This is why underinsurance can affect a burst-pipe, burglary or storm claim, not only a total loss. A later full guide can unpack average in detail; for now, the practical point is to keep the valuation basis and sum insured aligned.

A practical review rhythm for households and businesses

Review every sum insured at least at annual renewal and whenever a material change makes the old number unreliable. Automatic inflation adjustments can help, but they cannot know about every new solar system, renovation, high-value purchase, stock peak or growth plan.

Home and buildingsRenovations, extensions, pools, solar, generators, outbuildings, changed construction costs or a new professional valuation.
Household contentsMajor purchases, gifts, jewellery valuations, new electronics, home-office equipment or a move.
MotorRenewal, restoration, modifications, accessories, changed use, different mileage or an updated valuation.
BusinessNew equipment, rising stock, added premises, business growth, changed turnover, new contracts or a longer recovery period.

For contents, SAIA says regular reviews are essential to keep cover aligned with current replacement costs. For buildings, the 2022 ASAQS guidance recommends a proper replacement-cost valuation, especially where the rebuilding assumptions are complex. Keep schedules, inventories, photos, serial numbers, invoices and valuations together; they help you choose the amount now and prove the loss later.

If something has changed, use Best Care’s policy-change route. If you are comparing a new arrangement, its guide on comparing insurance policies can help you look beyond premium alone.

Four common misconceptions to remove from your schedule review

The safest reading is precise, not optimistic. These corrections prevent the most common leap from “number shown” to “outcome promised”.

“The sum insured is what I will automatically receive.”No. It is generally a cap or reference amount. The proven covered loss and all policy rules still apply.
“The purchase price is always the right insured value.”No. A building’s reinstatement cost, contents replacement cost and a vehicle’s defined insured value can all differ from what you paid.
“The insurer automatically updates every item’s value.”No. An index increase cannot identify your renovations, purchases, stock movements or changed circumstances unless you disclose them.
“Only a total loss is affected by underinsurance.”No. Where average applies, the proportional reduction can affect partial property losses too.

Key takeaways

  • The sum insured is generally a cap or calculation reference, not a guaranteed payout.
  • The schedule and full policy wording must be read together.
  • Replacement value, market value, agreed value and indemnity value are not synonyms.
  • Buildings, contents, motor, business property, interruption and liability use different valuation logic.
  • Underinsurance can reduce a partial claim when an average clause applies.
  • Review sums insured annually and after every material household or business change.

FAQs on sum insured meaning and policy schedules

These answers cover the general South African position, not the outcome under any one policy. Your schedule, wording and claim facts remain decisive.

What does ‘sum insured’ mean on my South African insurance policy schedule?

It is the amount recorded for a particular section, asset or interest and usually acts as the maximum or reference amount for a valid claim. It is not a guaranteed payout. The settlement still depends on the proven loss, valuation basis, excesses, limits, exclusions, conditions and the wording of your policy.

How is the sum insured different from my premium, excess and claim amount?

The premium is what you pay for cover. The excess is the part of an accepted claim you must contribute. The claim amount is the value of the loss you report and support with evidence. The sum insured is the section’s cap or reference value, subject to the policy wording.

How should I work out the correct sum insured for my home, contents and car in South Africa?

Use the basis stated in the policy. Buildings often need a full professional reinstatement value, including related rebuilding costs. Contents commonly need today’s cost to replace all items new. Motor cover may use retail, market, trade or agreed value. Ask your broker or insurer to confirm the method in writing.

What is underinsurance and how can the average clause affect my claim?

Underinsurance means the sum insured is lower than the value that should have been insured on the policy’s stated basis. If an average clause applies, a valid partial claim may be reduced in the same proportion. The exact formula, tolerance and order of deductions depend on the policy wording.

Does the insurer update my sums insured automatically?

Some policies apply an automatic annual increase, but that does not mean every renovation, purchase, valuation change or business expansion is known to the insurer. You remain responsible for checking the schedule, disclosing material changes and asking for updates when needed.

Why is a building insured for replacement value instead of its market value or purchase price?

Buildings insurance is generally concerned with the cost of reinstating the structure after insured damage, not the land or the price a buyer would pay for the property. Demolition, professional fees, municipal costs, construction and escalation can all affect that reinstatement value.

How often should I review my sums insured?

Review them at least at each annual renewal and after a material change. Triggers include renovations, solar installation, major purchases, new high-value items, changed vehicle use, higher stock levels, new equipment, business growth or a revised professional valuation.
